plan: In a second-price sealed-bid auction with independent private values, bidding one's true value is a dominant strategy regardless of what other bidders do. This is because if I bid higher than my value, I risk winning and paying more than the item is worth to me; if I bid lower, I risk losing a profitable opportunity. Since I pay the second-highest bid (not my own bid) when I win, there's no incentive to shade my bid. Therefore, my optimal strategy is to bid exactly my value of $31, regardless of my beliefs about Betty and Charles's strategies.

In a second-price auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: your payment depends only on the second-highest bid, not your own bid (given you win). Bidding above value risks winning and overpaying relative to value; bidding below value risks losing profitable opportunities. Since this holds regardless of competitors' strategies, the optimal action is straightforward truthful bidding. My value is $31, so I will bid exactly that amount to maximize expected profit.

This is a second-price auction (winner pays the second-highest bid), which is strategically equivalent to a Vickrey auction. In such auctions, bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy: bidding higher than your value risks winning and paying more than the item is worth to you, while bidding lower than your value risks losing profitable opportunities. Since other bidders are rational, they will also bid their true values, so my optimal strategy is simply to bid my true value of $46, regardless of my beliefs about their bids.
